displayQuote: If you don't think too good, don't think too much

meta.title: Who really said "If you don't think too good, don't think too much"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Ted Williams everywhere, but traceable only to a 2007 quote anthology. No date, no occasion, no primary source — and no sign it is wrong either.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you don't think too good, don't think too much'?
meta.ogDescription: Ted Williams, says every source — all of them downstream of one 2007 anthology. No date, no occasion, no primary record. Honestly thin.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · American baseball player — Boston Red Sox, 1939–1960
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Williams without exception, and it sounds exactly like him — a clubhouse wisecrack from the game’s most notorious over-thinker about hitting. But the paper trail is one line long. Wikiquote ↗ sources it to The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations (2007), edited by Wayne Stewart, at page 360, and that is a compilation: it records that the line circulates, not who said it, when, or to whom. We found no date, no game, no interview and no book of Williams’s own attached to it.

source.excerpt: If you don't think too good, don't think too much.
trail: Wikiquote’s Ted Williams page ↗ lists the line and gives exactly one citation for it: “As quoted in The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations (2007) edited by Wayne Stewart, p. 360.” Simple Wikiquote ↗ carries the same citation with the publisher and ISBN — Skyhorse Publishing, 160239072X.

The book is real: the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ gives The gigantic book of baseball quotations, associated name “Stewart, Wayne, 1951–,” New York: Skyhorse Pub., 2007, ISBN 9781602390720. The scan is access-restricted, so we could not read page 360 — but the citation points at a genuine book, not a phantom.

Quote Investigator has no article on it ↗ — a site search for “think too good” returns “Nothing Found.” On a line this widely repeated, the absence of a QI investigation means nobody has traced it, not that it has been cleared.

A phrase search of the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America newspaper archive ↗ returns zero hits for “if you don’t think too good”. That archive’s coverage runs well into Williams’s playing career, so a null result is worth reporting — though it is a partial corpus, and absence there is not proof of absence.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to give, and that is the finding. The line is printed as a free-standing aphorism in the 2007 anthology ↗ and reproduced from there; no source we read places it in a conversation, a game, an interview or a book.

sourceLink.text: The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations (Skyhorse, 2007)

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted. We cannot say where these words were first published: the only source we located is a 2007 anthology reprinting them, which tells us nothing about the original utterance or its date. quotle.info makes no public-domain claim — and note that the anthology itself, being from 2007, is firmly in copyright.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.heading: About Ted Williams
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · American baseball player — the last man to bat .400 over a full season
author.bio: Theodore Samuel Williams played nineteen seasons for the Boston Red Sox between 1939 and 1960, twice interrupted by service as a Marine pilot, and finished at .344 with 521 home runs, six American League batting titles and two Triple Crowns. In 1941 he hit .406, which nobody has matched over a full season since, and he was elected to the Hall of Fame on the first ballot in 1966. He was famous for thinking about hitting harder than anyone alive — he wrote a book about it — which is precisely why a line advising people not to think gets repeated in his name.

cite.sourceCitation: Wayne Stewart, ed., The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations (New York: Skyhorse Publishing, 2007), 360 — a quotation anthology, and the only source we could locate. No primary record of the remark is known to us.

misattribution.heading: How thin the trail is
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this line, and we are not taking it off Williams. But it is worth seeing what the citation everyone repeats actually is.

items.why: Wikiquote’s one source ↗ is The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations ↗, 2007. An anthology reprinting a saying is evidence that it was already circulating by 2007 — roughly half a century after Williams retired, and five years after he died. It is not evidence about the utterance.

items.who: No date, no game, no interview
items.why: Williams talked to reporters for decades and wrote two books about hitting. If this line has a moment attached to it, no reference we read names one — not Wikiquote ↗, not Simple Wikiquote ↗, not Wikipedia ↗.
Quote Investigator returns “Nothing Found” ↗ for the phrase, and Chronicling America ↗ returns zero hits. This is a line that has never been chased, not one that has been checked and cleared.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: this is almost certainly Ted Williams, and there is currently no way to prove it. If you need a quote you can defend, use his line about goals instead — that one at least reaches a book with his name on the spine.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke only works because of who is supposed to have made it. Williams was the most analytical hitter of his era — he used a lighter bat than most sluggers because it gave him a faster swing, and in 1971 published The Science of Hitting ↗, a book Wikipedia says is “still read by many baseball players”. Advice to think less, from him, lands as a needle rather than a platitude: it is the expert telling you that the method is not transferable.

That is also why it spread without a source. A line that sounds this much like its attributed speaker needs no provenance to be believed, which is exactly the condition under which quotations detach from evidence.
detailsBody: We put a real effort into dating it and came back with nothing, so here is the negative result in full: no Quote Investigator article; no hits in the Library of Congress’s digitised newspapers; no citation in Wikipedia’s biography ↗; and, in Wikiquote ↗, a single pointer to a 2007 anthology whose own page we could not open because the scan is access-restricted ↗. A reader with a library copy of that book could move this page forward in ten minutes.

Compare the treatment of Williams’s other famous line. “A man has to have goals…” gets cited to a specific page of his own autobiography — contested as to which page, but a real book with his name on it. This one gets cited to a book of quotations. The difference is the whole distinction between a documented quote and a well-liked one.
context.pull: A line that sounds right needs no source to be believed. That is the problem.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Ted Williams page lists "If you don't think too good, don't think too much." with the single source note "As quoted in The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations (2007) edited by Wayne Stewart, p. 360." No date or occasion is given.
Simple Wikiquote carries the same line citing The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations by Wayne Stewart, 2007, Skyhorse Publishing Inc, ISBN 160239072X, page 360.

The Internet Archive catalogue record for giganticbookofba0000unse gives title "The gigantic book of baseball quotations", associated name "Stewart, Wayne, 1951-", date 2007, publisher "New York : Skyhorse Pub.", ISBN 9781602390720 / 160239072X, 810 images, and access-restricted-item = true.
A Quote Investigator site search for "think too good" returns no articles — the page shows "Nothing Found: Sorry, but nothing matched your search terms."

A Chronicling America (Library of Congress) phrase search for "if you don't think too good" returns 0 results. (Verified via the collection's JSON endpoint; the HTML search page returns 403 to automated fetchers.)

Wikipedia gives Ted Williams (August 30, 1918 - July 5, 2002), Boston Red Sox 1939-1960, .344 career average, 521 home runs, .406 in 1941, six AL batting titles, two Triple Crowns, Hall of Fame 1966 on the first ballot, and The Science of Hitting (1971). It carries no citation for "If you don't think too good, don't think too much."
